results.title: fal published pricing for Audio and 3D model APIs — PricingSaaS Pulse
results.author: Rob Litterst
highlights:
## What changed

Per fal's pricing page as of Oct 1, 2026, the company rebuilt its model API pricing into per-endpoint tables: it published new Audio and 3D pricing tables, and expanded the Video and Image tables to 10 endpoints each — including H3 Max, Kling v3, Seedance 2, Nano Banana 2 and GPT Image 2 — dropping sample rows for Wan 2.5, Veo 3, Ovi, Seedream V4 and Qwen. Rates for overlapping models carried over unchanged, per the same Oct 1, 2026 page: Kling 2.5 Turbo remained $0.07 per second and Nano Banana remained $0.0398, and GPU rates were untouched as well.

...

For a product leader pricing a multi-modal AI product, this is a packaging move more than a pricing move: fal didn't change what anything costs, it changed how legible its catalog is. Splitting Audio and 3D into their own tables, and widening its Video and Image lineups, makes it easier for a buyer to compare a specific model's rate before committing — a level of per-endpoint transparency that's harder to pull off once a catalog gets this wide. Teams bundling many models under one metered rate should watch whether granular, per-endpoint pricing pages become

...

## In context

fal has tracked pricing since Jul 27, 2026, and this is only its second real change, coming 59 days after it raised the H100 GPU list price from $3.99 to $4.50 per hour on Aug 3, 2026. This time fal rebuilt its model API pricing into per-endpoint tables rather than touching a dollar figure, publishing new Audio and 3D tables and widening its Video and Image tables. Price reveals like this are common across the companies Pulse tracks — most are first-time price disclosures like Contractzen's Sep 28, 2026 reveal of a $15/mo AI add-on price or Postscript's Sep 28, 2026 reveal of $699/mo AI Plan pricing, rather than a company rebuilding an entire pricing table the way fal did. For fal, the move reads as transparency catching up with scope — the table now matches how many modalities the API actually serves.

results.title: Report: Fal AI Business Breakdown & Founding Story | Contrary Research
results.author: Emre Karaarslan
highlights:
### Serverless and Compute Pricing

Source: fal

Fal charges for Serverless and Compute by GPU time on its own fleet, quoting both a list rate and a discounted rate per chip. As of September 2026, H100 capacity starts at $1.90 per hour against a list rate of $4.50, while B300, the newest chip on the fleet, starts at $4.50 against a list rate of $8.50. The spread between list and discounted pricing is where volume commitments are negotiated.

...

### Cost Drivers

Fal's dominant cost is GPU capacity, and it carries that cost in two forms. It rents from cloud providers, and it operates its own colocated fleet across 35 data centers as of December 2025, which means paying for headroom that sits idle between demand spikes. The second cost is the research team writing kernels, which is the work the inference engine depends on and a fixed cost that does not scale down with usage. Fal has not disclosed gross margin, so how much of the optimization advantage reaches the income statement is not publicly checkable.

...

Fal offers access to B300, B200, H200, H100, and RTX PRO 6000 chips across its Serverless and Compute platforms, both renting GPUs from cloud providers and operating its own collocated infrastructure. As of December 2025, it was running in 35 data centers. For fal's workloads H200 chips are considered "overkill", and the company has been moving from H100 directly to B200 and B300 for better performance per watt and per dollar. However, there have been supply limitations. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang confirmed in December 2025 that Blackwell chips were sold out through mid-2026, against a backlog of 3.6 million units from the largest cloud providers alone. Fal's exclusive reliance on Nvidia silicon concentrates that exposure.

In this context, capital can become a competitive weapon by allowing capacity to be bought ahead of demand and allocated against a backlog the biggest committed buyers reach first. Fal's total funding of $337.5 million as of September 2026 is less than a quarter of what either Fireworks AI or Baseten raised in a single 2026 round. Fal's business rests on converting an optimization advantage into a price and performance advantage. If GPU costs rise faster than it can pass them through, or if a better-funded rival buys the same capacity cheaper and funds the same media-specific kernel work, the advantage compresses from both directions at once. Batuhan Taskaya has argued that fal's exclusive focus on generative media is what keeps that gap open while competitors stay oriented around language models.

## How does fal pricing work?

fal meters at two distances from the hardware. Serverless compute is raw capacity, a GPU-hour rate card with six SKUs from RTX PRO 6000 at $4.00/h list to B300 at $12.99/h list, each shown with its VRAM and an "As low as" rate, with H100 at $2.49/h. Model APIs are priced on outcomes, per output unit, and the unit follows the modality: seconds for H3 Max and Kling video, 1000 tokens for Seedance 2, images and megapixels for Nano Banana and FLUX.1 [schnell], 1000 characters or seconds for audio, and units, generations or credits for 3D. Output pricing fits generative media because customers think in clips, images and voice lines, and the "Units per $1" column, 20 seconds of H3 Max Reference to Video, 333.33 megapixels of FLUX.1 [schnell], 5,000 seconds of ACE Step audio, puts every unit on one scale.

...

Under the hood, the two rate sheets reveal two billing engines. GPU hours are a classic rate table with a list price and a floor, and the "As low as" column, paired with "Contact Sales", points to negotiated rates tied to volume or commitment, with the spread running from $5.99/h against $12.99/h on B300 to $2.49/h against $4.50/h on H100. Model APIs are output metering with pass-through economics: each endpoint carries its own rate in the unit its lab meters, and the footnotes show the math, an average video of 5 seconds at 720p, images normalized to 1MP with "Higher resolutions will be priced proportionally", and a note that some models "may use GPU-based pricing depending on architecture". Worth borrowing: when a catalog spans many units, a normalized value column with its assumptions printed underneath gives the buyer one comparison to make.

results.title: Inference Is Priced Like Software but Spent Like Hardware | AInvest
results.author: Anders Miro
highlights:
The two fastest-rising private AI companies of the past year do not build models. Fireworks AI just raised $1.505 billion at a $17.5 billion valuation, and Fal - the startup that powers image and video generation inside tools like Canva and Perplexity - is negotiating a round at around $8 billion. Both sell inference: the act of running a trained model to produce an answer, an image, or a video every time a user asks. Each autocomplete Cursor finishes and each image Canva renders is an inference event billed against somebody's GPUs.

...

The part worth pausing on is what that revenue is made of. To run their clouds, the startups buy Nvidia NVDA-- silicon and resell the compute at a markup. Fal lists its serverless H100s at $1.90 an hour against a $4.50 list price - the business is a spread over a chip it leases from Nvidia, a strategic investor in Fireworks and a participant in Fal's Series D. Blackwell chips were sold out through mid-2026. The $1.5 billion Fireworks raised and the $300 million to $350 million Fal is after are not line items in a software budget; they are the price of locking up datacenter capacity before a rival does. In plain terms, the rounds are sized like a hardware business while the valuations are being priced like a software one.

That gap does the analytical work. $17.5 billion is roughly 17 times Fireworks' stated revenue run rate; Fal's $8 billion is 20 times its $400 million. Software companies 861053-- earn multiples like that when revenue is high-margin and repeatable. Whether that applies here is exactly what no one discloses. None of the major inference providers publishes gross margin or cohort retention, so the figures in the open - revenue, run rates, token counts - cannot yet separate a durable business from a subsidized resale. The untested question is how much of each dollar survives the cost of the chips, and whether customers keep coming back after their first project. Open-source models are free to self-host, and that ceiling on inference prices is the standing threat to every revenue dollar in the category.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Jump 22% in a Month as GPU Shortage Hits Firms and Labs - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: An Hye-ji, Intern Reporter
highlights:
■ Surging GPU costs: Demand for artificial intelligence computing has climbed sharply, prompting domestic cloud providers to raise graphics processing unit rental rates following similar moves by U.S. neocloud companies. Unlike the past, when rental rates for older products fell as new ones arrived, prices for previous-generation GPUs are rising as well, making the ability to secure computing resources a decisive factor in the success of AI businesses and research.

...

- Key summary: Vessl AI, a domestic neocloud company, raised the hourly rate for Nvidia H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39 on the 1st of this month, a 24.7% increase. The price adjustment marks the start of similar moves in Korea after U.S. neocloud firms including CoreWeave and Nebius successively raised GPU rental rates. Vessl AI procures most of its roughly 7,000 GPUs through leasing. According to Ornn, an AI computing trading platform, the hourly cloud rental rate for the H100 rose 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, reaching about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. The impact is spreading to industry and research, with some companies abandoning bids for government-led AI transformation projects because they could not secure GPUs, while universities and research institutes scale back the size of their research.

results.title: Rental Rates for Older AI Chips Jump 25% as Demand Surges - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Seo Ji-hye, Kim Ji-young
highlights:
Vessl AI raised its hourly rate for Nvidia H100 graphics processing units by 24.7% starting this month, following a string of price increases by U.S. neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius amid a surge in demand for artificial intelligence computing. Supply has tightened not only for the newest chips but also for older models as demand for high-performance GPUs jumps. Other Korean cloud providers also expect to raise GPU rates depending on supply conditions, raising concerns that higher costs of securing GPUs will weigh on service development at Korean AI companies and on government AI transformation, or AX, projects.

Vessl AI on the 1st raised the hourly rate for H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39, according to AI industry sources on the 21st. The neocloud company counts leading Korean AI firms including Upstage and Motif Technologies among its clients and currently operates several thousand GPUs. It has secured about 7,000 GPUs, most of them leased rather than purchased outright. "It is hard to secure the volume we need for H100s — effectively, the price is whatever the seller names," a Vessl AI official said. "As AI demand grows, the number of customers wanting to use GPUs keeps rising, so a price adjustment was unavoidable." The company plans to expand its GPU fleet to about 10,000 units by the end of the year, but intends to keep adjusting rates flexibly to reflect supply conditions and procurement costs.

Other Korean AI cloud companies, including Elice, have also raised prices recently. In the past, rental rates for older AI GPUs fell when new models arrived, but prices for previous-generation chips are now rising as well. Hourly cloud rental rates for the H100 climbed 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, according to Ornn, an AI compute trading platform. That is about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. Analysts say demand is spilling over to relatively older GPUs because supply of the newest chips cannot keep pace with surging computing demand.
